section.title: Lead the project while preserving room to build
section.deck: Jake Bolam describes large infrastructure migrations, accessible technical leadership, protected focus time, and a deliberately risk-sensitive review style.

blocks.question: What was your path from joining Meta to principal engineer?
answer: Bolam joined at IC6 in Facebook Groups during early pandemic remote onboarding. With election work limiting teammates’ availability, he had a slow start. His manager helped represent that context in reviews. He later moved to Instagram Web, closer to the UI and React work he had intended to do, and could contribute immediately.

followups.question: Was your performance at risk during the slow onboarding?
answer: He remembers a satisfactory rather than exceptional rating and thinks his manager’s explanation of the slow onboarding mattered. He does not claim that every slow ramp is automatically protected.

followups.question: What was your background before Meta?
answer: He began with frontend work but repeatedly moved into frontend and then backend infrastructure. He hoped a large company would let him specialize in product UI; the same pattern recurred. Experience made infrastructure easier for him to influence, and the larger server platform offered a greater impact surface.

blocks.question: Why did your managers offer you leadership across several teams?
answer: He had already told them he wanted career growth and had led several teams before Meta. The organization needed coordination during a stack migration, and a strong first month demonstrated readiness. He was offered an opportunity to stretch from one team to multiple teams; he still had to deliver the project rather than treat the assignment itself as a promotion.

blocks.question: What do IC7 and IC8 scope mean in your kind of work?
answer: In his lens, IC6 often leads one team and IC7 works across teams or a broader area; IC8 extends the reach further. The significance of the problem also matters. Framework work affecting thousands of engineers can have substantial scope even without a corresponding reporting structure. He explicitly recognizes another path through deep specialists whose small code changes produce very large savings. These are examples, not fixed team-size rules.

blocks.question: Did you deliberately choose a leadership archetype?
answer: Not especially. He tries to do what the project needs while leaning on strengths in communication, coordination, and creating a team people enjoy working with. He wants others to succeed and thinks that can compound across a long project. He does not usually think in the host’s “force multiplier” label.

followups.question: Why not management?
answer: He has tried short management stints but wants the option to write a large amount of code when needed. He also prefers having managers who can check his occasional careless remarks. His preference combines the technical work he enjoys with awareness of interpersonal responsibilities.

blocks.question: Why remain available to colleagues despite senior responsibilities?
answer: Accessibility reveals ideas and problems that might otherwise remain invisible and helps people move forward. He may have to defer a meeting when overloaded, but tries to find a route to help.

followups.question: How do you decide whom to give time?
answer: He tries to ignore levels, including for interns. Genuine questions and acting on advice encourage further investment. When he lacks time, he may defer or connect someone to a better-informed colleague. This is an attempt to balance access with limited capacity.

followups.question: What makes a good question?
answer: Be sincere about what you want to understand rather than script an impressive interaction. A real question makes it easier to identify the right person, including someone else with more time or expertise.

blocks.question: What work drove the IC7 and IC8 promotions?
answer: For IC7, a migration originally thought to take roughly two years achieved most of its work in about six months. That freed most resources for other work, including ads on Instagram Web. He credits the team rather than claim individual ownership of the speedup.

For IC8, leadership trusted him with the much harder move of Instagram’s backend into the main Meta stack. Many engineers initially saw no reason to leave a familiar, effective environment. Instead of beginning with a demanded migration, the team improved developer experience between the stacks, then added missing Instagram capabilities to the destination.

Over several years, crossing the boundary became easier, more surfaces moved for their own benefit, and demand shifted toward completing the migration. Major surface and traffic milestones demonstrated scope before the entire program was finished. He describes approximately one hundred fifty involved teams and meaningful performance or development improvements, while leaving exact credit and promotion decisions to their broader context.

followups.question: How did a two-year migration become a six-month effort?
answer: They cut scope, changed the strategy, and developed team momentum. Moving pages in larger batches rather than one at a time created difficult initial integration work but then allowed compounding progress. The team played to individual strengths and became convinced it could move sooner.

followups.question: How did you make the team excited?
answer: He cannot fully explain an organic process or take all the credit. He brought energy, colleagues reinforced one another, and people enjoyed shared progress. Finishing earlier benefited the whole team and enabled valuable subsequent work.

blocks.question: How did you keep developers satisfied during the infrastructure change?
answer: A server-champions group connected representatives from across the organization, with product engineers making up most of the participants. That kept infrastructure grounded in everyday development. A continuing feedback channel often revealed trouble within hours, earlier than broad complaint groups where issues had to become severe before someone posted. Metrics complemented, rather than replaced, those relationships.

blocks.question: How did your work hours change as responsibility increased?
answer: Hours fluctuate with excitement and the project: he sometimes works sixty or seventy hours, then deliberately returns toward forty or less during another period. He wants a life beyond work and attributes recent balance to systems developed across his career. The pattern is personal, not an assertion that a particular average guarantees principal-level impact.

followups.question: Which systems protect that time?
answer: He reserves roughly half the week for focus, avoids morning meetings because mornings suit him, aims for no meetings on Wednesdays and Fridays, and groups one-on-ones on Monday afternoons. Tuesday and Thursday afternoons can then hold project discussions. Exceptions occur; the value is a protected default, not rigid adherence.

followups.question: What changes during a concentrated coding period?
answer: He cancels many meetings for a few weeks once work has momentum and people know the plan. His projects may have necessary workstream meetings without layers of central recurring syncs. Lead coordination happens when needed through direct conversations or broader forums, and he remains reachable for urgent questions.

followups.question: Do you also review code during those periods?
answer: Yes. He checks pending reviews before his own coding and revisits them frequently because waiting for approval can block another engineer. Review is part of moving the project forward, rather than an interruption to personal output.

blocks.question: How do you decide the depth of a code review?
answer: He scales effort to risk. Core architecture, live production changes, and system-wide decisions receive thorough attention. A gated, isolated leaf component can receive a much lighter review because its failure or rewrite is contained. He still looks for conspicuous hazards. He calls this controversial and acknowledges that it differs from many colleagues’ expectations.

followups.question: What if someone actually wants a deeper review?
answer: Authors can flag that in the summary or return an approved change for more scrutiny. Their signal can correct his assessment of risk or indicate a desired design discussion. The approach also depends on team trust; new colleagues do not immediately receive the same assumptions.

followups.question: Why ask how to accept rather than how to reject?
answer: He wants to identify real blockers rather than require code to match his personal style. Experienced engineers can recognize multiple workable forms. His unusual extension is to approve with a clear warning even when a fix is mandatory, trusting known colleagues to correct it before landing. He says that has not caused the feared production failure in his experience, while asking unfamiliar authors to return when ready. This is an attributed team practice, not a recommendation to treat known defects as safe.

blocks.question: How do you judge whether you are moving too quickly?
answer: He uses production feedback and metrics to adjust. If a rollout is healthy and brings little negative signal, he may increase exposure faster than conventional increments; if problems appear, he pulls back. The host and Bolam agree that some risk accompanies speed, while daily breakage suggests too much. The transcript does not establish that absence of complaints proves absence of harm; it records the signal-based judgment he describes.

blocks.question: Do you use AI?
answer: He uses ChatGPT often outside work and internal tools at Meta. He sees them as useful tools with mistakes and caveats, and thinks engineers should learn to use available capabilities. The calculator analogy expresses enthusiasm about adoption rather than a claim that model outputs are equally reliable.

blocks.question: What is a tech lead responsible for?
answer: The project’s success, in his view. Usually the most useful action is aligning people and ensuring they contribute in the right direction, but the lead may need to write code or debug a problem no one else can resolve. He gives an example of spending weeks tracing an elusive bug. The role is flexible contribution to the outcome rather than a single activity.

followups.question: What mistake do new technical leaders make?
answer: They can become absorbed in daily operations and lose sight of the goal, especially when the surrounding direction changes. The lead must notice and redirect the team rather than continue executing an obsolete plan.

blocks.question: How do you balance coding with wider leadership?
answer: He usually writes some code weekly to stay in the complete toolchain, often taking a task he can finish far faster than someone else. Focus blocks help. But he may stop coding for weeks when reviews, resource planning, or another activity offers greater value. The aim is useful allocation, not preserving a coding quota.

followups.question: How do you learn what is worth your time?
answer: Experience helps. An earlier heuristic was to seek work he believed important that nobody else would do. He now recognizes that neglected work can also be neglected because it is unwise, so the judgment still needs scrutiny. He also reserves time for useful contributions that may not appear in performance-review credit, including helping colleagues and maintaining technical contact.

blocks.question: What is your note-taking system?
answer: A separate VS Code window contains plain-text files in one large folder, named for people, projects, and priorities. He navigates by fast filename search, adds dates and times through shortcuts, and writes frequent notes because memory is unreliable. He avoids elaborate filing. Links between files provide connections; a graph view is interesting but not central. The archive includes work and personal thoughts accumulated for years.

followups.question: Do you maintain an achievement diary for reviews?
answer: Not consistently. He did so for one year but usually reconstructs achievements later, acknowledging the cost of spending a day on that reconstruction. His existing notes serve current thinking more than daily credit accounting. The host suggests launch posts as another record because they already need to be written, and Bolam likes that idea.

blocks.question: What advice would you give a new graduate version of yourself?
answer: Go where your strengths are valued. Someone good at frontend, debugging, or frameworks can be ineffective in a role whose leaders need a different contribution. A poor review does not automatically mean those strengths are worthless; recognizing the mismatch and moving can change both performance and enjoyment. He also advises being kind, simple, and able to enjoy work as oneself.

followups.question: What is the cost of bringing an informal personality to work?
answer: He sometimes says something unwise. He tries to acknowledge it and apologize promptly, while relying on an established reputation for good intent. He does not treat authenticity as permission for extreme or harmful remarks.

steps.text: Reduce pain in existing cross-stack work.
